name: CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD
amazonQuery: CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD pure sine wave UPS
summary: A 1500VA / 1000W pure sine wave tower UPS with 12 outlets and USB-C charging, the default pick for gaming PCs and workstations with active PFC power supplies.
verdict:
The CP1500PFCLCD is the UPS to buy for a modern desktop computer: a true sine wave on battery and the highest watt rating of the common 1500VA towers.

**The 1000W rating is the point.** Most 1500VA units are rated at 900W. CyberPower rates this one at 1500VA / 1000W, which gives a gaming PC more headroom. A practical rule is to keep the load under about 80% of the watt rating, so plan for 800W or less. A 450W PC plus two 30W monitors and a 20W router comes to about 530W, well inside that line.

**Runtime is minutes, not hours.** The spec sheet lists about 10 minutes at half load (500W) and 2.5 minutes at full load. That is enough to save your work and shut down, which PowerPanel software can do on its own over the USB data cable. Light loads last much longer, as the [run time](/glossary/run-time/) glossary explains, so a 60W router and NAS stack rides through far longer outages.

**Pure sine on battery.** Active PFC power supplies can click off or buzz on a stepped waveform. This unit outputs a [pure sine wave](/glossary/pure-sine-wave/) and is line-interactive with AVR, so it fixes brownouts without touching the battery. Current units add one USB-A and one USB-C charge port.

Owners praise the clear LCD and quiet operation. The main complaint is the sealed lead-acid battery, which needs replacing every three to five years. It is the top pick in our [best UPS battery backup](/best-ups-battery-backup/) guide; if you want the APC equivalent, compare the [APC BR1500MS2](/gear/apc-back-ups-pro-br1500ms2/), or step down to the [CP1000PFCLCD](/gear/cyberpower-cp1000pfclcd/) for lighter loads.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the CP1500PFCLCD and the CP1500AVRLCD3?
faqs.a: Both are 1500VA line-interactive towers with 12 outlets. The CP1500PFCLCD is rated at 1000W and outputs a pure sine wave on battery. The CP1500AVRLCD3 is rated at 900W and outputs a simulated sine wave, which suits network gear and TVs but not every active PFC power supply.

name: APC Back-UPS Pro BR1500MS2
amazonQuery: APC Back-UPS Pro BR1500MS2 sine wave UPS
summary: APC's 1500VA / 900W sine wave tower with 10 outlets and USB-A plus USB-C charging, a strong home office pick for PCs, monitors and network gear.
verdict:
The BR1500MS2 is the APC answer to the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD, and it is the better fit for a home office that wants built-in device charging.

**Sine wave, but 900W.** APC rates it at 1500VA / 900W with sine wave output on battery and a line-interactive design with AVR. That covers a typical office PC, two monitors, a dock and a router with room to spare: 250W + 60W + 30W + 20W is about 360W, or 40% of the rating. For a heavy gaming rig near 700W, the 1000W [CP1500PFCLCD](/gear/cyberpower-cp1500pfclcd/) has more margin.

**Outlet layout matters.** There are 10 outlets: 6 battery-backed with surge protection and 4 surge-only. Put the PC, monitor and router on the battery side, and printers or speakers on the surge side. Laser printers draw large spikes and should never go on a battery outlet.

**USB-C on the front.** It adds one USB-A and one USB-C charge port, so a phone or tablet charges straight from the battery during an outage. The LCD shows load, battery level and estimated [run time](/glossary/run-time/), and PowerChute software can shut the PC down over USB.

Owners like the tilting display and the USB-C port. Complaints center on fan noise under load and the weight, about 28 lb. It ranks second in our [best UPS battery backup](/best-ups-battery-backup/) roundup. If you do not need the sine wave, the [APC BX1500M](/gear/apc-back-ups-pro-bx1500m/) has the same capacity in a simpler box.

name: CyberPower CP850PFCLCD
amazonQuery: CyberPower CP850PFCLCD pure sine wave UPS
summary: An 850VA / 510W pure sine wave UPS with 10 outlets, a compact fit for office desktops, small NAS boxes and home networks that never pull 500W.
verdict:
The CP850PFCLCD gives you the same pure sine wave as CyberPower's 1500VA flagship in a smaller, lighter box, and for most office desktops it is all the UPS you need.

**Do the watt math first.** CyberPower rates it at 850VA / 510W. Add up your gear: an office PC at 150W, two monitors at 25W each and a modem and router at 20W comes to about 220W, roughly 43% of the rating. A gaming PC under load can pass 510W on its own, and then the UPS will alarm and cut over to bypass, so that is a job for the [CP1500PFCLCD](/gear/cyberpower-cp1500pfclcd/).

**Runtime at small loads.** The spec sheet lists about 11 minutes at half load (255W) and 2 minutes at full load. The battery is a single 12V 9Ah sealed lead-acid pack. At a 60W network load you can expect far longer, since runtime climbs quickly as load falls; the [run time](/glossary/run-time/) glossary explains why.

**Clean power where it counts.** It outputs a [pure sine wave](/glossary/pure-sine-wave/) on battery and is line-interactive with AVR. There are 10 outlets, 5 battery-backed and 5 surge-only, plus a 1,150-joule surge rating and USB for PowerPanel shutdown software.

Owners like how quiet and compact it is. The main complaint is short runtime near full load. It is the compact pick in our [best UPS battery backup](/best-ups-battery-backup/) guide; the [CP1000PFCLCD](/gear/cyberpower-cp1000pfclcd/) is the step up if you sit near 400W.
bestFor: Office desktops and home networks that draw under 400W
skipIf: You run a gaming PC that can pull more than 500W

name: CyberPower CP1500AVRLCD3
summary: A 1500VA / 900W simulated sine wave UPS with 12 outlets and USB-A plus USB-C charging, a value pick for routers, network gear, TVs and game consoles.
verdict:
The CP1500AVRLCD3 is the best value 1500VA UPS for network gear and home theater, but it is the wrong choice for a modern PC with an active PFC power supply.

**The waveform is the trade.** On paper it matches the pricier models: 1500VA / 900W, line-interactive with AVR, 12 outlets (6 battery-backed, 6 surge-only). On battery, though, it puts out a simulated sine wave rather than a [pure sine wave](/glossary/pure-sine-wave/). Routers, modems, switches, TVs and game consoles do not care. Some active PFC PC power supplies do, and may shut off at the moment of transfer.

**Lots of runtime for small loads.** CyberPower lists about 12 minutes at half load (450W) and 3 minutes at full load. A modem, router, mesh node and switch together often draw 40W, a small fraction of the rating, so the same battery covers a far longer outage. Use the [run time](/glossary/run-time/) guide to estimate yours.

**Useful extras.** It adds two USB charge ports (a 2.4A USB-A and a 15W USB-C), RG6 coax surge protection and a USB data port for PowerPanel shutdown software. It weighs 23.8 lb.

Owners praise the price and the outlet count. The main complaint is from PC users whose power supplies click off on battery. It is the value pick in our [best UPS battery backup](/best-ups-battery-backup/) guide. For a computer, spend a bit more on the [CP1500PFCLCD](/gear/cyberpower-cp1500pfclcd/).
bestFor: Routers, network switches, TVs and game consoles
skipIf: You are protecting a PC with an active PFC power supply
pros: Coax surge protection for cable modems
cons: Simulated sine wave can trip some active PFC power supplies

faqs.q: Is the CyberPower CP1500AVRLCD3 OK for a gaming PC?
faqs.a: Not ideal. It outputs a simulated sine wave on battery, and some active PFC power supplies in gaming PCs shut down or buzz on that waveform. It is rated at 900W, so capacity is fine. For a PC, the pure sine CP1500PFCLCD is the safer choice.

faqs.q: How long will the CP1500AVRLCD3 keep a router and modem running?
faqs.a: Much longer than its headline runtime. CyberPower lists 12 minutes at half load, which is 450W. A modem and router typically draw 15 to 30W, a tiny fraction of that, so expect well over an hour in most homes. Runtime is not linear, so check the LCD estimate once connected.

name: APC Back-UPS BE600M1
amazonQuery: APC Back-UPS BE600M1 UPS battery backup
summary: A 600VA / 330W standby UPS with 7 outlets and a USB charging port, the simple, affordable way to keep a modem and router online in an outage.
verdict:
The BE600M1 is the UPS to buy for your internet equipment, and it does that one job very well for very little money.

**Small rating, small loads.** APC rates it at 600VA / 330W. That sounds small until you add up a network: a cable modem at 10W, a router at 12W and a mesh node at 8W is 30W, under 10% of the rating. APC's own runtime examples list about 4.3 hours for a 10W modem and router and about 30 minutes for an 80W laptop and gateway. Use the [run time](/glossary/run-time/) guide for your exact load.

**Standby, simulated sine.** This is a standby design with a simulated sine wave output, not line-interactive. Network gear and laptop chargers handle that fine. A desktop PC under load can pass 330W, and some active PFC supplies dislike the waveform, so pair a desktop with a [CyberPower CP850PFCLCD](/gear/cyberpower-cp850pfclcd/) or larger.

**Sized for a shelf or wall.** There are 7 outlets: 5 battery-backed and 2 surge-only. A USB-A port (1.5A) charges a phone during an outage. It weighs about 7.7 lb, has keyhole slots for wall mounting next to the modem, and carries a 3-year warranty.

Owners like how easy it is to set up and hide. The main complaint is the loud beeping on power loss, which you can silence. It is the router pick in our [best UPS battery backup](/best-ups-battery-backup/) guide, and the [CyberPower EC850LCD](/gear/cyberpower-ec850lcd/) is the next size up.

faqs.a: Several hours. APC's runtime examples list about 4.3 hours for a modem and router drawing around 10W. Most home networks draw 15 to 30W, which still gives one to several hours. Add a mesh node or a PoE camera and the runtime drops, so check the total wattage first.

faqs.q: Can the APC BE600M1 run a desktop computer?
faqs.a: Only a light one. It is rated at 330W, and it is a standby unit with a simulated sine wave. A basic office PC and monitor may fit, but a gaming PC under load can exceed 330W, and some active PFC power supplies dislike the waveform. Use a pure sine model for a desktop.

name: Tripp Lite SMART1500LCDT
amazonQuery: Tripp Lite SMART1500LCDT UPS battery backup
summary: Tripp Lite's 1500VA / 900W line-interactive tower with 10 outlets and a PWM sine output, a solid small-office UPS for PCs, phones and network gear.
verdict:
The SMART1500LCDT is a dependable small-office UPS, though for a home buyer the CyberPower and APC 1500VA picks offer more for similar money.

**Ratings that match the class.** Tripp Lite, now part of Eaton, rates it at 1500VA / 900W, line-interactive with AVR. The spec sheet lists about 10 minutes at half load (450W). That covers an office PC, two monitors and a phone system long enough to shut down cleanly. For long network-only outages, a 60W load runs far longer; see [run time](/glossary/run-time/) for the math.

**PWM sine, not pure sine.** On utility power it passes a sine wave. On battery it outputs a PWM sine wave, a stepped approximation. Most computers handle it, but if you have a modern active PFC power supply and want certainty, the [CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD](/gear/cyberpower-cp1500pfclcd/) outputs a [pure sine wave](/glossary/pure-sine-wave/).

**Office extras.** It has 10 outlets, 5 battery-backed and 5 surge-only, a 650-joule surge rating, and Tel/DSL and Ethernet surge protection, which is handy for VoIP and DSL lines. The LCD shows input voltage, load and remaining runtime. It weighs 27 lb and carries a 3-year warranty in the US.

Owners like the informative display and the quiet fan. The common complaint is the lower joule rating and the lack of USB charging ports. It is the small-office pick in our [best UPS battery backup](/best-ups-battery-backup/) guide; buy it where your office already standardizes on Tripp Lite or Eaton.

name: APC Back-UPS Pro BX1500M
amazonQuery: APC Back-UPS Pro BX1500M UPS battery backup
summary: A 1500VA / 900W line-interactive tower with 10 outlets and AVR at a lower price than APC's sine wave model, best for network gear and older PCs.
verdict:
The BX1500M is APC's value 1500VA tower: the same capacity as the BR1500MS2 in a simpler box, with a stepped waveform that suits everything except some modern PC power supplies.

**Capacity and runtime.** APC rates it at 1500VA / 900W, line-interactive with AVR. Retail spec sheets list about 10.9 minutes at half load (450W) and 2.8 minutes at full load. For a home network at 40W, expect far longer. The [run time](/glossary/run-time/) glossary explains why runtime grows so fast as load drops.

**Know the waveform.** On battery it outputs a stepped approximation to a sine wave, not a [pure sine wave](/glossary/pure-sine-wave/). Routers, switches, TVs, consoles and older PCs run fine. Some active PFC power supplies in newer gaming PCs may click off at transfer. If that is your machine, the [APC BR1500MS2](/gear/apc-back-ups-pro-br1500ms2/) or [CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD](/gear/cyberpower-cp1500pfclcd/) is worth the step up.

**The layout.** It has 10 outlets, 5 battery-backed and 5 surge-only, a 789-joule surge rating, an LCD with load and runtime, and a USB data port for PowerChute shutdown software. It weighs 24.25 lb and recharges in about 16 hours, so back-to-back outages can find it partly charged.

Its appeal is the price and APC's software. The drawbacks are the long recharge time and the stepped waveform. See how it compares in our [best UPS battery backup](/best-ups-battery-backup/) guide; the [CyberPower CP1500AVRLCD3](/gear/cyberpower-cp1500avrlcd3/) is its closest rival.

That is the usual job of a desktop UPS: ride through flickers and give you time to save and shut down, which PowerPanel can do automatically over USB. At about 15.4 lb, it is far easier to move than a 1500VA tower.

name: CyberPower EC850LCD
summary: A light 850VA / 510W standby UPS with 12 outlets and ECO-controlled outlets that cut idle peripherals, a budget fit for home networks and basic PCs.
verdict:
The EC850LCD is a cheap, light UPS with more outlets than you would expect, and it suits home networks and basic office PCs rather than gaming rigs.

**Ratings and runtime.** CyberPower rates it at 850VA / 510W. The datasheet lists about 10.4 minutes at 210W and 2.15 minutes at 425W. A modem, router and small NAS at 50W will run for much longer. If your load is a basic office PC and monitor at about 150W, you have time to save and shut down. The [run time](/glossary/run-time/) guide shows how to estimate your own.

**Standby, simulated sine.** It is a standby design with a simulated sine wave on battery, no AVR stage. Network gear, TVs and laptop chargers do not mind. For a modern PC with an active PFC supply, the pure sine [CyberPower CP850PFCLCD](/gear/cyberpower-cp850pfclcd/) is the safer match at the same rating.

**The ECO outlets.** There are 12 outlets: 6 battery-backed and 6 surge-only, 4 widely spaced for bricks. Three surge-only outlets are ECO-controlled: with the USB cable connected, the UPS switches them off when your computer sleeps or shuts down, killing standby draw from speakers and printers. It also protects an RJ11 phone line, carries a 526-joule surge rating and weighs only 7.7 lb.

Its appeal is the low price, light weight and outlet count. The limits are the standby design and a short full-load runtime. It sits between the [APC BE600M1](/gear/apc-back-ups-be600m1/) and the bigger towers in our [best UPS battery backup](/best-ups-battery-backup/) guide.

name: APC Smart-UPS SMT1500C
summary: APC's 1500VA / 1000W pure sine Smart-UPS with 8 battery-backed outlets and SmartConnect cloud monitoring, built for home servers, NAS boxes and small offices.
verdict:
The SMT1500C is a business-grade UPS for a home lab, NAS or small-office server, and it costs more than consumer towers because every outlet is battery-backed and the monitoring is far better.

**Every outlet is protected.** APC rates it at 1500VA / 1000W with a [pure sine wave](/glossary/pure-sine-wave/) output and line-interactive AVR. All 8 outlets are battery-backed; there are no surge-only outlets to plug the wrong device into. Retail spec sheets list about 7 minutes at full load. At 300W, a NAS, switch and small server, you can expect several times that. Check your own load with the [run time](/glossary/run-time/) guide.

**SmartConnect is the reason to pay more.** The C suffix means a SmartConnect port that reports to APC's cloud portal, so you can see battery health, load and outage events from a phone. There is also a SmartSlot for an optional network card and a USB port for shutdown software. That makes it a fit for a server closet you do not visit every day.

**The trade-offs.** It is a big, heavy tower, and it costs far more than a consumer 1500VA unit. APC lists a 3-year unit warranty and a 2-year battery warranty. It is not expandable, so you cannot add a battery pack for longer runtime.

Its appeal is the all-battery outlet layout and remote monitoring. The drawback is price. For a gaming PC alone, the [CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD](/gear/cyberpower-cp1500pfclcd/) gives the same 1000W rating for much less; see our [best UPS battery backup](/best-ups-battery-backup/) guide.
